newsitem.title: HUNGARY: BB DEAL UPGRADES HUNGARY BANK SALES - MINISTRY.
newsitem.headline: BB DEAL UPGRADES HUNGARY BANK SALES - MINISTRY.

text.p: The recent adjustments on the Budapest Bank privatisation contract showed that the assessment of Hungary and its bank sale programme improved substantially over the past one year, the Finance Ministry said on Thursday.

Hungary sold considerable stakes in most of its large banks in the past two years and plans to complete the bank privatisation programme by the end of 1997, with selling K&H, Hungary's third largest bank, and several smaller banks.
"The buyers of (Budapest Bank) have recognised that a favourable turnaround had happened in the situation of the country and the bank," Secretary of State Tibor Draskovics told a news conference.

GE Capital Services, which has operational control of the bank, bought a 27.4 percent stake in Budapest Bank (BB) in December 1995. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, which is a financial investor, has 32.4 percent, and the Hungarian state 22.8 percent.

The government had to face a fusillade of political attacks over BB's privatisation, with the opposition parties accusing the Finance Ministry of selling the bank with conditions unfavourable to the state.

Draskovics said Hungary was in a bad bargaining position in the sale, a much-needed breakthrough for the lagging bank privatisation at a time when Hungary's 1995 economic austerity programme was yet to gain investors' confidence.

But the programme brought substantial improvement in the performance of the economy in 1996 and Hungary could meet the budget requirements undertaken in a stand-by loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund last March, he addded.
Pressured by the political attacks on the BB sale, the Finance Ministry acquired last year the permission of GE and the EBRD to publish the details of the sale contracts.
The details, however, were not published for weeks. The reason for the delay was that Prime Minister Gyula Horn initiated the renegotiation of certain points of the contracts.
The parties agreed to the changes on December 23, including the repurchase of BB's loss-making Polgari unit for some 1.1 billion forints ($6.8 million).

The deal happened earlier than the state undertook in the original contract. The state originally guaranteed to buy back assets worth up to 8.25 billion forints, or some 3.5 percent of BB's assets, in 1997 and 1998.

Further changes, affecting the conditions of the asset repurchase and mainly the abolishment of a state guarantee for buying back all the BB shares if the bank loses 50 percent of its assets in three years, substantially improved the state's position, Draskovics said.
